explanations.explanation: Yes, friend, the call goes out wide: "Hear, O peoples, all of you; listen, O earth, and everyone in it!" (Micah 1:2). That's every people and everybody on the earth, with nobody left standing in the back. When a message starts like that, you put down your spatula and listen.

The temple is in the verse, but it's in a different spot. The text says the Lord is speaking "…from His holy temple." (Micah 1:2). The one called to listen is "…earth, and everyone in it!" So the temple is where the Lord speaks from, and the earth is who's listening.

I can see why a city sounds right, since two cities show up soon in this passage. But the call in Micah 1:2 is bigger than any one city: "listen, O earth, and everyone in it!" That's the whole earth, with every address included. No single city gets to sit this one out.

That's it, friend. "The mountains will melt beneath Him… like wax before the fire" (Micah 1:4). I've watched a cookie box get left by the oven and I'm telling you, a mountain doing that is a whole different thing. The picture shows how great the LORD is when He comes down.
Bowing is a nice guess, but that's not the word in the text. The mountains "…melt beneath Him…" (Micah 1:4). The picture is wax before the fire. Wax going soft and running is what the verse shows.

Going up is the opposite direction. The LORD comes down and treads on the high places, and the mountains "…melt beneath Him…" (Micah 1:4). Nobody's getting taller here. A mountain that's melting is losing height, not gaining it.

Right on target, baker. "…the valleys will split apart…" (Micah 1:4). So the mountains melt on top and the valleys crack open down below. Picture a cookie that cracks straight down the middle when it comes out of the oven, only this is a whole valley.
That would be a pretty fix, but the text doesn't go there. It says the valleys "…will split apart…" (Micah 1:4). Nothing gets built up in this verse. The ground is coming apart.

Dust is a good guess, since things do fall apart here. But the verse says the valleys "…will split apart, like wax before the fire, like water rushing down a slope." (Micah 1:4). Split is the word. The water picture is there too, but dust isn't.

Yes, friend. "All this is for the transgression of Jacob and the sins of the house of Israel." (Micah 1:5). The melting and splitting aren't random. The text ties them straight to those sins. Then it asks what the transgression of Jacob is, and answers with Samaria.

Edom isn't mentioned anywhere in these verses, friend. The verse names the cause plainly: "…the transgression of Jacob and the sins of the house of Israel." (Micah 1:5). The message points at Jacob and Israel. Pride is a fine word, but Edom isn't the one it's about here.

Assyria never shows up in these verses, friend. The text says, "All this is for the transgression of Jacob and the sins of the house of Israel." (Micah 1:5). That's the cause the verse gives. Look for the answer that matches those words.

explanations.answer: A planting area for a vineyard
explanations.explanation: That's the one. The message says Samaria will be "…a heap of rubble in the open field, a planting area for a vineyard." (Micah 1:6). Think about that, friend. A whole city, and the spot ends up as a place to plant vines.

explanations.answer: A pasture for flocks of sheep
explanations.explanation: Sheep would fit a field, I'll give you that. But the text says "…a planting area for a vineyard." (Micah 1:6). That's a place for planting, and no flock is mentioned. The verse gives a vineyard.

explanations.answer: A camp for an army of soldiers
explanations.explanation: An army camp sounds like something that would follow a ruined city, but the verse doesn't say it. Samaria becomes "…a heap of rubble in the open field, a planting area for a vineyard." (Micah 1:6). Vines, not tents. I think that's a pretty quiet ending for a city.

Yes, friend, idols is the one. Verse 7 says, "…I will destroy all her idols." It also says that all her carved images will be smashed to pieces (Micah 1:7). So the idols are on the list of what goes down along with the city.
Horses show up later in the passage, when Lachish is told to harness its chariot horses (Micah 1:13). But in verse 7, what gets destroyed is "…all her idols." Different verse, different list.
No ships anywhere in this passage, friend. Verse 7 says, "All her carved images will be smashed to pieces… and I will destroy all her idols." Idols are what go down, not a fleet.

True. Right after the word against Samaria comes "Because of this I will lament and wail…" (Micah 1:8). The words come in a first-person voice, and the text doesn't say whose voice it is, so I'll leave that open too. What I can tell you is that grief comes right on the heels of the judgment.

It's actually true, friend. The line right after the word against Samaria is "Because of this I will lament and wail…" (Micah 1:8). The judgment in verses 6 and 7 doesn't end on a cold note. A cry of grief follows it straight away.

Not quite, friend. The text says the opposite: "it has reached even Judah; it has approached the gate of my people, as far as Jerusalem itself." (Micah 1:9). The wound doesn't stop at Samaria's border. It keeps coming, all the way to Jerusalem's gate.

Right, it's false. Micah 1:9 says the wound "…has reached even Judah; it has approached the gate of my people, as far as Jerusalem itself." It doesn't stop at Samaria. It keeps on going until it's at Jerusalem's door.

That's right, baker. The text says, "Shave yourselves bald and cut off your hair in mourning for your precious children…" (Micah 1:16). Children are called precious right there in the verse. That tells you this mourning is a deep one.
Battle isn't the reason the verse gives. The text says it's "…in mourning for your precious children…" (Micah 1:16). This is about grief. It's a heavy line, so let's stick with what the verse says.

explanations.answer: To keep a vow to the LORD
explanations.explanation: The verse doesn't mention a vow anywhere. It says the shaving is "…in mourning for your precious children…" (Micah 1:16). I'd rather stick with the reason the text gives, friend. This one is about grief.
Yes, friend. The children "…will go from you into exile." (Micah 1:16). That's the reason for the mourning, and it's a heavy one. I think this is one of those lines you read slowly.

Battle is a natural guess, but it's not the word in the verse. The text says the children "…will go from you into exile." (Micah 1:16). Exile means being taken away from home. That's what the mourning is for.
Hiding isn't the word in the verse. The children "…will go from you into exile." (Micah 1:16). The text says they go from their people into exile. It's a heavy line, and I think it's meant to be.
